newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt aims blow at militants by mass trials.
newsitem.headline: Egypt aims blow at militants by mass trials.

text.p: Egyptian courts are trying more than 150 suspected Moslem militants in three simultaneous cases that activists say are part of the government's bid to show it has the upper hand in the bloody war with Islamists.

The latest trial opened on Sunday when 22 men and a juvenile appeared before a State Security Court on charges of planning attacks targeting police, tourists, journalists, artists and ministers. Prosecutors charge the men had received military training abroad.
The defendants bring to 152 the number of alleged members of the militant al-Gama'a al-Islamiya (Islamic Group) -- Egypt's largest militant group -- before Cairo courts.

"The fact that so many militants are on trial at the same time could be an attempt by the government to show foreign investors that it has overcome militant violence and that Egypt is a safe place," said Hisham Mubarak, executive director of the Centre for Human Rights Legal Aid.

"The government may consider these trials the final chapter in its war with the militants. These look like the last big trials. The police have made big gains in the attempt to wipe out the danger of the Islamists and militant attacks are small and confined to areas outside the capital."

Police say they have broken the back of the military wing of the Gama'a through raids on its hideouts and steps to prevent the organisation from receiving help from abroad. The number of Gama'a attacks has declined sharply since the mid-1990s.
Most of defendants in the three cases face charges related to incidents that date from 1994, one of the bloodiest years in the militant campaign against the government.
Yasser el-Serri, an Egyptian militant in exile in Britain, said the government had a "store" of militants in detention that it put on trial every now and then as a show of force.

"Most of those on trial have been in store for a long time and the government pulls them out whenever it needs to show it is in control and has the upper hand," said Serri, sentenced to death in absentia for trying to kill the prime minister in 1993.

The current trials include the largest in Egypt of alleged militants, involving 97 men and women before a military court on charges that include planting bombs outside nine banks in 1994 and the daring assassination of the head of the government's anti-militant squad in the same year.

Violence has decreased since then. According to figures published by the Egyptian Organisation for Human Rights, 174 people died in political violence in Egypt in 1996, down from the 373 deaths it recorded in 1995.

EOHR's annual report said that although the war with Islamists had lost some of its intensity in 1996, the government used the violence as an excuse to refer dozens of civilians to military court and to detain hundreds more illegally.
"This (military) trial is a signal from the government to those inside and outside Egypt that all is under control, from both the security and judiciary angle," EOHR's Mahmoud Kandil told Reuters.

Activists say the government sent a similar message earlier this year when parliament, dominated by the ruling party, approved a presidential decree to extend for three more years the emergency law in force since Moslem militant army officers assassinated President Anwar Sadat on October 6, 1981.

Prime Minister Kamal Ganzouri, who has engineered a successful privatisation programme, said the latest extension of the law, which gives security forces broad powers of arrest and detention, was aimed at protecting the economy from sabotage by "terrorists".

President Hosni Mubarak in 1992 cleared the way for military courts to try civilians in a bid to nip in the bud a growing militant campaign to topple his government. The courts, known for their swift and harsh sentences, have sent dozens of militants to the gallows.
But despite its recent low profile, the Gama'a has not completely disappeared.

Suspected Gama'a members shot dead six policemen in one attack earlier this month. Many of the group's influential leaders live abroad and disagree with a call for a truce with the government that was issued by imprisoned leaders.
